title: The book found (2 Kings 22)
hookLine: a lost scroll is found in the Temple, and the prophetess Huldah is consulted
last: THE WEEPING WAS PART OF THE PRAYER.

cards: Dust, scaffolding, money changing hands. King Josiah has sent his scribe, Shaphan, to the Temple to sort out payment for the carpenters, builders and masons doing repairs. It's a building job.

Then the high priest, Hilkiah, hands the scribe something and says: "I have found the book of the Law in the house of the LORD." He calls it the book of the Law, found inside the house of the Lord itself.

teach.h: SHAPHAN READS IT TO THE KING.
teach.b: Shaphan reads it and carries it to the king. He gives his report on the builders first, then, almost in passing, mentions the scroll and reads it aloud.
When Josiah hears the words of the book, he tears his clothes, and gives his reason in his own words: our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book. So he does something careful.
He doesn't act alone on his first reaction.
He sends the high priest, the scribe and others to inquire of the Lord, and they go to a woman: Huldah the prophetess, who lives in Jerusalem.
The text gives her almost no introduction, only her husband's family and where she lives. Then it gives her the floor. Her answer has two parts.

The hard part: the trouble the book describes will come. The tender part is for Josiah himself: because your heart was tender, and you humbled yourself when you heard, and tore your clothes and wept, I have heard you.
You'll be gathered to your grave in peace. What was the scroll? The text just calls it the book of the law.

Some readers suggest it was Deuteronomy, or part of it, and the text doesn't settle the question. What it shows is the moment of finding. A people had the words in their own house and had lost track of them.
In the story, the find works less like a treasure than like a mirror. And instead of filing it away, the king listened, wept, asked a prophet, and took it seriously.

how: Jews read the finding of the book as part of the book of Kings, and Huldah is remembered in Jewish tradition among the prophetesses of Israel.

games.q: you're King Josiah. an old scroll has just been read to you, and it alarms you. what do you do?
o: act at once on your own reading.
send people to ask a prophet what it means.
have it put back where it was found.
games.why: Josiah sends them to inquire of the Lord, and they go to Huldah the prophetess.

practice: Rest your hands open, as if holding a page, and think of words you already own but haven't read in a long time: a psalm, a prayer from childhood, a blessing on a wall, a letter from a grandparent.
Say a few of its words slowly in your head, and ask what they ask of you now that you'd forgotten. If you pray, you can hold those words before God.

wordCard.voice: Huldah, the prophetess King Josiah sent his officials to when the long-lost book of the law was found and read to him.

orig.note: Hebrew: the book of the law (the Torah), as Hilkiah calls the scroll he found.

carryVoice: Your line: a mirror, not a treasure. The words were in the house all along. Seven hundred eighty days now.
